In pre-IFHRMS scenario, Department of Finance (DoF) manually collected budget requirement details from Heads of Departments (HoDs) in Compact Disks and carried out budgeting activity in Microsoft Access.

IFHRMS envisaged standardisation of budget operations with less manual efforts, real-time budget control, monitoring and analysis. However, audit observed that improved decision making for Budget Transfer and re-appropriations was not achieved due to absence of processing controls which allows transfer of funds between Grants, incurring of expenditure without budget provision and withdrawal of budget provision after incurring expenditure as discussed in the succeeding paragraphs.

3.2.1 Budget allocation

Budget allocation and additional funds sanctioned through Additional Sanction Ledger (ASL) are distributed to all Budget Control Officers (BCOs) by HoDs through ‘budget transfer’ sub-module in IFHRMS. BCOs in turn distribute them to DDOs under their control. Workflow analysis revealed the following shortcomings:

(i) Budget Manual stipulated that budget should not be transferred from one grant to another grant. Test check, however revealed that IFHRMS budget transfer process allows transfer of funds between HoDs irrespective of the

Government replied (January 2023) that budget transfer process is designed in such a way that it will not allow re-appropriation of budget from one grant to another. The reply was not acceptable, as budget transfer process allows transfer of funds between HoDs without any validation to restrict transfer of funds only between the HoDs of respective grants. As a result there is a likelihood of funds getting transferred between HoDs across different grants, which contravenes clause 143(i) of Budget Manual.

Recommendation 4:

Government should strengthen budget module to prevent transfer of funds between grants by strictly enforcing provisions of budget manual.

(ii) When budget allocation is transferred initially or during re-allocation of funds between DDOs, the availability of funds is known only on generation of Budget availability report. 33

Samagra–2 scheme, creating new livelihood opportunities.

And the proposed system will also enable jurisdiction-wise assignment of appeals to the respective Appellate Authorities, stage-wise monitoring of prescribed timelines, electronic communication, maintenance of complete audit trails and generation of management and BRAP compliance reports. This will facilitate effective monitoring of the appeal mechanism at the State level and ensure uniformity in its implementation across all Planning Authorities.

5. In view of the above, the Commissioner of Town and Country Planning has requested the Government accord approval in principle for establishing and implementing the Online Appeal and Dispute Resolution System through the Single Window Portal and to issue suitable orders incorporating the appeal and dispute resolution provisions for online filing, processing, hearing, disposal, monitoring and disclosure of appeals relating to planning/building permission applications, for adoption by Commissioner of Town and Country Planning, Chennai Metropolitan Development Authority and all other Planning Authorities concerned in the State.

Postnatal care is crucial for ensuring the

health and well-being of both the mother and the

newborn during the critical period following

To strengthen postnatal care and promote newborn health, Mother and Baby Care Kits containing essential items such as baby clothing, bedding, mosquito nets, hygiene products and newborn care materials are provided to mothers delivering in Government health facilities. This initiative promotes institutional deliveries, exclusive breastfeeding, infection prevention and improved newborn care practices.

During the year 2025–26, 4.12 lakh Mother and Baby Care Kits were distributed. During the year 2026–27 (April and May), 63,725 kits were distributed.

The Government of Tamil Nadu will continue to strengthen postnatal care services through timely postnatal visits and home-based care for mothers and newborns. It will further promote exclusive breastfeeding, essential newborn care practices and awareness of neonatal and maternal danger signs to facilitate the early referral of complications and improve maternal and neonatal health outcomes.

338

6.7. Menstrual Hygiene Programme (MHP)

Menstrual hygiene is a significant public health issue affecting adolescent girls and women due to limited access to sanitary napkins, inadequate awareness and socio-cultural stigma. Poor menstrual hygiene contributes to reproductive tract infections, school absenteeism, reduced participation in daily activities and adverse reproductive health outcomes. Evidence from the National Family Health Survey (NFHS) and other public health studies highlights the importance of menstrual health education and access to sanitary napkins in improving dignity, health and well-being.

The Menstrual Hygiene Programme (MHP), implemented in Tamil Nadu since 2011, aims to promote safe menstrual hygiene practices, improve reproductive health awareness and ensure equitable access to sanitary napkins for adolescent girls and women.

Under the programme, free sanitary napkins are provided to adolescent girls aged 10–19 years who have attained puberty, school and college students, out-of-school girls, postnatal mothers,

women prisoners and women admitted to Government health facilities.

The programme is implemented by the Directorate of Public Health and Preventive Medicine in coordination with the Directorate of School Education and the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS). Distribution is carried out through Schools, Colleges, Anganwadi Centres and Government health facilities, along with awareness activities on menstrual hygiene management and environmentally safe disposal practices.
